common_name: Bloodshot Eyes Wild Ginger (Alabama Wild Ginger)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring at the same depth they were growing, in humus-rich woodland soil in light to full shade, and keep the crowns evenly moist until new leaves harden off.

directions: This selection was collected from a wild population in Autauga County, Alabama and is grown for its wide-eyed, owl-like spring flowers, which open larger and flatter than most Asarum blooms in shades of tan, purple, and maroon. The triangular evergreen leaves carry a fine silvery overlay and release an anise-like scent when bruised. It forms a tidy, slowly expanding clump rather than running, and performs best where summer heat is reliable and winter drainage is good.

planting.note: Plant small divisions shallowly in spring in well-drained woodland soil in light to full shade; this cultivar tolerates root competition and drier shade better than most wild gingers once established.

directions: A compact selection rescued from a Wake County, North Carolina site, this is one of the smallest garden wild gingers, forming dense mats of near-black, heart-shaped leaves overlaid with bright silver veining. Maroon-and-white flowers hide beneath the foliage in late spring and are best appreciated by parting the leaves. Because it handles dry shade better than the larger Asarum species, it is a good edging or rock-garden choice under established trees where irrigation is limited.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, humus-rich woodland soil in part sun to light shade; the thick creeping rhizomes need several seasons to fill in but eventually form a substantial patch.

directions: Native to China, this is among the largest-flowered wild gingers in cultivation, producing oversized blooms with a striking white ring set between dark purple outer petals and an even darker purple throat. The glossy leaves can reach 8 inches long and are carried on thick rhizomes that slowly colonize the surrounding bed. It tolerates more filtered sun than most Asarum species, making it a useful patterned-foliage groundcover at a woodland bed's brighter edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in light shade in fast-draining, humus-rich soil; this Hubei-Province species comes from bamboo-shaded slopes below 1,000 feet elevation and prefers steady warmth over cold, wet winters.

directions: This dwarf Chinese selection carries glossy, triangular leaves randomly blotched with lighter green, forming a low evergreen carpet. In late winter and early spring, thimble-shaped, creamy flowers rimmed in dark purple emerge at ground level beneath the foliage. It is well suited to a raised woodland bed or trough where its fine detail can be seen up close, and it is generally left alone by deer and rabbits.

planting.note: Plant dormant rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in early spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in part shade; growth emerges quickly once soil warms and dies back again by midsummer.

directions: This robust selection of the Himalayan mayapple emerges each spring with strongly mottled, reptilian-patterned red-and-green leaves that gradually turn solid green and fade by midsummer as the plant goes dormant. Cup-shaped pink flowers appear in May at the leaf axils, followed by egg-shaped red fruit by midsummer. It grows noticeably taller and more vigorously than the typical wild-collected species, making a bolder textural statement in a shaded border.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in rich, well-drained woodland soil in part sun to shade, giving each plant several feet of room to spread its outsized leaves.

directions: A 2012 hybrid of Podophyllum boreale and P. difforme introduced by Juniper Level Botanic Garden, this is one of the largest mayapples grown, with thick stems holding jaggedly cut leaves that can reach 25 inches across. Clusters of two dozen or more small red flowers dangle just beneath the foliage, and unlike most Podophyllum it continues producing flushes of bloom from March into September rather than a single spring show. Its scale and long bloom season make it a dramatic anchor plant for a large shaded bed.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade; unlike the American mayapple this clumping species does not run and holds its leaves well into fall.

directions: Selected from crosses of plants collected in Taipei and Taichung Counties, this Taiwanese mayapple forms a clump of just two, but enormous, glossy, deeply lobed leaves with a tropical, almost caladium-like presence. In April, dangling clusters of shredded, beet-red flowers hang below the foliage, followed by ornamental fruit later in the season. It stays in a tight clump rather than colonizing by rhizome, which makes it a good choice for a defined specimen spot rather than a groundcover role.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained woodland soil in part sun to shade; this northern subspecies tolerates more open sky than the typical species without scorching.

directions: This is a distinct, more cold- and sun-tolerant northern race of the Chinese umbrella mayapple, carrying broad, mottled, umbrella-like leaves atop sturdy stems. Deep red flower clusters form beneath the leaf canopy in spring, mostly hidden from view until the foliage is parted. It has become an important parent in modern Podophyllum breeding programs because it passes on both its hardiness and its tolerance for brighter exposure to its hybrid offspring.

planting.note: Divide clumps or plant container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part sun to light shade, tolerating full shade once established.

directions: Collected in India rather than the more typically encountered Chinese forms, this evergreen selection sends up bamboo-like shoots tinted purple as they emerge in early spring, branching into a multi-stemmed clump. Unlike the species, which typically flowers white, 'Indian Purple' produces dark purple, bell-shaped flowers in late spring that stand out clearly against the foliage. It is a distinctive, drought-tolerant addition to a dry-shade woodland planting once its roots are established.

common_name: Ki Naka Fu Dwarf Fairy Bells

planting.note: Plant divisions shallowly in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in light shade to full shade; the rhizomes creep gently and are best interplanted among ferns or hostas rather than grown as a solo specimen.

directions: This dwarf Japanese and Korean selection is grown chiefly for its variegated foliage, with each small leaf marked by a golden-yellow center edged in thin green streaks. Tiny, star-shaped white flowers appear just above the foliage in early spring, followed by small berries. Because it stays low and spreads gently by rhizome, it works well as an interwoven groundcover companion beneath taller shade perennials rather than as a stand-alone accent.

common_name: Low Man Dwarf Evergreen Solomon's Seal

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright shade to full shade; this dwarf form spreads slowly into a low mat and is well suited to edging a shaded path.

directions: This dwarf cultivar of the Chinese evergreen Solomon's-seal relative stays much shorter than the typical species, forming a dense, low, spreading mat rather than an upright clump. Small, dangling, bell-shaped flowers appear beneath the arching foliage in spring, and the glossy leaves persist through winter in milder zones, unlike deciduous Polygonatum. It has proven resistant to the sawfly larvae that often disfigure true Solomon's seal, making it a reliably tidy choice for a shaded rock garden or path edge.
